442.title: The thunder glorifies
442.hook: the thunder glorifies His praise, and the angels too, in awe (13:13)
442.howItsDone: When they hear thunder, some Muslims pause and repeat the words reported from 'Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr in Malik's Muwatta: glory be to the One whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels in awe of Him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'ibra, the lesson you cross over into. The story is the lesson.

A summer storm at night. The flash first, so bright the room goes white. Then you start counting, the way kids do: one, two, three. Then the sound, rolling across the roof, rattling the windows, so deep you feel it in your chest. Grown adults still flinch. Surah thirteen of the Qur'an is named for that sound. Ar-Ra'd: the thunder. And it hears something in that sound besides noise.

Verse twelve, in paraphrase: it is He who shows you the lightning, bringing fear and hope, and raises the heavy clouds. Fear of the strike, hope of the rain; for people in a dry land, both are real. Then verse thirteen, in Pickthall's translation: "The thunder hymneth His praise and (so do) the angels for awe of Him." The thunder isn't just a noise here. It's praising. The Qur'an says this in more than one place: another surah says there is nothing that doesn't glorify God with praise, but you don't understand their praise. Elsewhere it names the birds and the mountains among those that praise. Scholars read it in different ways. Some take it as real praise, in a language people can't follow. Some take it as the praise of a creature simply being what it was made to be. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi describes thunder as an angel charged with the clouds, and scholars discuss the strength of that report. Imam Malik records that 'Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr, a companion, would stop talking when he heard thunder, and say: glory be to the One whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels, in awe of Him. Some Muslims still say his words during a storm. A frightening sound, heard as praise, and a conversation paused out of respect, the way talk stops when someone nearby starts to pray.

segments.voice: Listen to whatever sound is around you: rain or wind if you have it, or traffic, a fan, the hum of a fridge. Don't name it; just listen, the way you'd listen to someone praying in another room. If you pray, you can say Ibn az-Zubayr's words, or simply subhanallah, glory be to God.
Ar-Ra'd. The surah named for the thunder: verse thirteen says it hymns God's praise, and the angels too, in awe.
Your line: the thunder is praising. A loud sound, heard another way. That's day four hundred forty-two.

443.title: Change what is in yourselves
443.hook: Allah does not change a people's state until they change what is in themselves (13:11)
443.howItsDone: Muslim preachers and reformers often quote 13:11 when calling a community to inner renewal, and some teach it alongside 8:53 as a principle that a people's outward state follows its inward one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ar-Ra'd, the thunder that hymns God's praise, and the angels too, in awe.

God helps those who help themselves. It sounds like scripture, and people quote it as if it were. It isn't in the Qur'an, and it isn't in the Bible either; it's an old proverb that Benjamin Franklin's almanac helped make famous. But there's a verse in ar-Ra'd that people often reach for when they mean something like it, in speeches, in sermons, on classroom walls. Read slowly, it says something more searching.

Verse eleven opens with a picture: every person has angels in front and behind, guarding them by God's command. Then, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts". In Arabic, the last words are ma bi-anfusihim: what is in themselves, in their own souls. Pickthall says hearts. Notice it's not about effort. The proverb says: work hard, and God will help. The verse says: what's inside a people, their intentions, their habits of mind, their honesty, shapes what happens to them. The outer condition follows the inner one. And it's plural: a folk, a people. Families, towns, nations, not just one person's self-improvement. Commentators point out the verse cuts both ways. A similar verse in al-Anfal says God never changes a blessing He's given a people until they change what is in themselves. A people can lose a good condition by what they let grow inside them, just as they can rise by turning. And the very next words in ar-Ra'd say that when God wills a hardship for a people, nothing can turn it back. So the verse isn't a guarantee that self-improvement brings success. It's a statement about where change has to begin. Modern Muslim reformers have quoted it when calling their communities to inner renewal.

segments.voice: Notice one habit of mind that shapes your days: a story you keep telling yourself, a suspicion you bring into every room, a habit of comparing or complaining. Don't attack it; just see it clearly, and choose one small thought to put in its place. If you pray, ask God to help you change what is inside.

444.title: Hearts at rest
444.hook: in the remembrance of Allah hearts find rest (13:28)
444.howItsDone: Muslims practice dhikr after the daily prayers and through the day, repeating phrases such as subhanallah, alhamdulillah and la ilaha illallah, often counting on the fingers or on prayer beads; Sufi orders also gather for dhikr together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ma bi-anfusihim, what is in themselves, and the line that change starts inside.

It's late. The house is quiet, the phone is face down, and your mind is doing laps. The email you didn't answer. The thing someone said at lunch. The bill. Back to the email. Nothing is broken. The heart just won't settle, like a glass of water on a table that keeps getting bumped. Surah ar-Ra'd has a verse for that hour. It's short, and it doesn't promise the email goes away.

Verse twenty-eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Who have believed and whose hearts have rest in the remembrance of Allah. Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" The key word is tatma'innu, find rest, from itmi'nan, a settled calm, the stillness of something that has stopped shaking. It's the same root as the soul at rest at the end of Surah al-Fajr, which you met last year. It appears in al-Baqarah too, when Ibrahim asks God to show him how He gives life to the dead. God asks: do you not believe? Ibrahim says: yes, but so that my heart may be at rest. Even a prophet wanted that settling. The means is dhikr, remembrance: calling God to mind in the prayer, in reading the Qur'an, and in short phrases repeated through the day. Subhanallah, glory be to God. Alhamdulillah, praise belongs to God. La ilaha illallah, no god but God. Notice the shape of the verse. It says the remembrance of Allah twice, and in the second half the Arabic puts those words before the verb: it is in God's remembrance that hearts find rest. Some commentators read that order as emphasis: there, and not elsewhere. Another verse adds a promise that runs both ways: remember Me, and I will remember you. And a hadith in Bukhari puts it starkly: the one who remembers his Lord and the one who doesn't are like the living and the dead. The verse doesn't say the world calms down. It says the heart can. The glass can stop shaking, even while the table is still being bumped.

445.title: If you are grateful
445.hook: if you are grateful I will surely increase you (14:7)
445.tomorrow: The good word, the good tree
445.howItsDone: Muslims express shukr by saying alhamdulillah, by thanking people, and by using blessings well; some perform a prostration of thanks, sujud ash-shukr, on receiving good news.

segments.voice: Yesterday: itmi'nan, the settled calm of hearts at rest, the last day in ar-Ra'd.

Surah fourteen is named for Ibrahim, but a few verses in, it's Musa who speaks. He tells his people, the Children of Israel: remember. Remember God's favor when He saved you from Pharaoh's people, who tormented you and killed your sons. Then he passes on a sentence God Himself had proclaimed. It's about a word you met on day eleven of this path, when you learned the difference between praise and thanks. Today, the thanks gets its own verse.

Verse seven. In Pickthall's translation, your Lord proclaimed: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more". In Arabic: la'in shakartum la-azidannakum. The grammar is emphatic, a promise with an oath folded in: if you are grateful, I will surely, surely increase you. And the other side: if you are ungrateful, the punishment is severe. The word there is kafartum, from kufr. Its root means to cover, the way a farmer covers a seed with soil; another verse, 57:20, uses the same word for farmers. Ingratitude covers a gift up, as if it weren't there. Shukr is the opposite. Classical scholars such as ar-Raghib describe it as showing a favor's effect, letting the gift be seen. Al-Ghazali and others describe three parts: in the heart, recognizing the gift came from God; on the tongue, saying so; in the limbs, using the gift well. And people are included. A hadith in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi says: whoever does not thank people has not thanked God. Remember a name you met last year: ash-Shakur, the Appreciative, one of God's names in the Qur'an. God, who needs nothing, is described as appreciating the small good people do, and multiplying it. So what is the increase? Scholars read it widely: more of the blessing, more blessings, more of the gratitude itself, a heart that sees more. They disagree about which, and some say all. What they share is the direction. Gratitude doesn't just answer the gift. It grows it.

segments.voice: Let three specific gifts come to mind: not my family, but the way your sister laughed on the phone yesterday. Hold each for a few breaths and recognize it in your heart; if you pray, say alhamdulillah, or thank God in your own words. Then think how you might use one of them well, with your hands.
Shukr. Gratitude: recognizing a gift, saying so, and using it well. Its opposite, kufr, covers the gift up. Today's word.
Your line: gratitude grows it. In the heart, on the tongue, in the hands. See you tomorrow.

446.title: The good word, the good tree
446.hook: a good word is like a good tree, roots firm, branches in the sky, fruit in every season (14:24–25)
446.carry: a good word is a tree
446.howItsDone: Muslim teachers explain 14:24–26 with the date palm hadith, and many read the good word as the testimony la ilaha illallah; the hadith 'a good word is charity' is widely taught to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shukr, and the promise in Surah Ibrahim: if you give thanks, I will give you more.

Medina. A group of companions sits with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and he gives them a riddle. There's a tree, he says, whose leaves don't fall, and it's like a believer. What tree is it? The grown men start guessing desert trees, one after another. In the circle sits a boy, 'Abdullah, the son of 'Umar. He thinks he knows. But he looks around at the older men, at his own father, and he's too shy to say it. Bukhari keeps the scene. The answer is a tree, and so is today's verse.

The answer was the date palm. Ibn 'Umar told his father afterward, and 'Umar said he'd have loved it if his son had spoken up. Now the verse, Surah Ibrahim twenty-four and twenty-five, in Pickthall's translation: "Seest thou not how Allah coineth a similitude: A goodly saying, as a goodly tree, its root set firm, its branches reaching into heaven, Giving its fruit at every season by permission of its Lord?" A goodly saying: kalima tayyiba, a good word. Many commentators, following Ibn 'Abbas, say the good word is the testimony at the heart of Islam: la ilaha illallah, no god but God. Its roots go down into the heart, its branches go up in good deeds, and it gives fruit all year. Others read it more widely: any good word, any true and kind speech. Both readings are old. Then verse twenty-six gives the opposite: a bad word is like a bad tree, torn up from the surface of the earth, with no hold at all. A good word, once said, keeps growing. The thing a teacher said when you were twelve. The sentence from your grandmother you still repeat. The kind remark from a stranger that got you through a week. And a bad word? It feels powerful when it's said, but it has no roots. It blows away, though not before it does damage. A hadith in Bukhari puts it simply: a good word is charity.

Kalima tayyiba. A good word, like a good tree: roots firm, branches in the sky, giving fruit in every season. Today's word.
Your line: a good word is a tree. Every sentence plants something. That's day four hundred forty-six.

447.title: Ibrahim at the House
447.hook: make this city safe, and make me and my offspring keep up prayer (14:35–41)
447.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Ibrahim's words from 14:40–41, rabbi j'alni muqima s-salati, in the final sitting of the daily prayer before the closing salam, and parents often say them for their children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kalima tayyiba, the good word that grows like a tree, roots firm, branches in the sky.

You met Hajar in the valley months ago, near the start of this path: a mother, a baby, a water skin, and a man walking away who said God had commanded it. Surah Ibrahim goes back to that valley from the other side, the father's. It keeps his prayer, line by line. A long report in Bukhari has him saying part of it as he walked away that day; the prayer also thanks God for two sons given in old age, so commentators differ over when each line was said. Either way, you overhear a father's whole list of requests.

Listen to what he asks for, in order. First: my Lord, make this city safe. Not rich, not famous. Safe. Then: keep me and my sons from worshiping idols; they have led many people astray. Then, in verse thirty-seven, in paraphrase: our Lord, I have settled some of my children in a valley with no crops, by Your sacred House, so that they may keep up the prayer. So make the hearts of people yearn toward them, and provide them with fruits, so that they may be grateful. He doesn't ask for fruit first. He asks for hearts: people's hearts, turning toward a valley with no crops. Then he thanks God for giving him Isma'il and Ishaq in his old age. And then the line in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Make me to establish proper worship, and some of my posterity (also); our Lord! and accept the prayer." And last: our Lord, forgive me, and my parents, and the believers, on the day the reckoning is set up. Some Muslims recite those last two verses near the end of their own prayer, just before the closing greetings. So a father's words at the House come back inside the prayer of people who face that same valley. He asked that his children would keep the prayer, and his words are said in it.

If you pray, recite Ibrahim's words or ask in your own language; if not, simply hold them in mind with care.

448.title: We will guard it
448.hook: We sent down the reminder and We will guard it (15:9)
448.howItsDone: Muslims keep copies of the Qur'an on high shelves, often wrapped in cloth, and handle them after wudu; worn-out copies are buried or respectfully disposed of, never thrown away.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibrahim's prayer at the House. And a week ends: thunder praising, change from inside, hearts at rest, thanks that grows, a good word like a tree.

A new surah, al-Hijr, and it opens with an insult. Verse six, in paraphrase: they say, you, the one the Reminder is sent down to, you are surely mad. Why don't you bring us angels, if you're telling the truth? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a man with a message and few people on his side. Three verses later comes the answer.

Verse nine, in paraphrase: it is We who sent down the Reminder, and it is We who will guard it. Listen to the Arabic pile up emphasis: inna nahnu, truly We, We ourselves, sent it; wa inna lahu la-hafizun, and truly, for it, We are guardians. Every part of the sentence says: this isn't on your shoulders. To a mocked man in Mecca, that's comfort before it's doctrine. The book's survival doesn't depend on whether the crowd believes him today. The Reminder, adh-dhikr, is one of the Qur'an's names for itself, the thing that brings to mind what people forget. Last year you met the huffaz, the memorizers, whose title comes from this verse's root. Muslim teachers point to the guarding at work through them, through the written copies gathered under Abu Bakr and 'Uthman, and through something smaller: how a copy is treated in an ordinary home. The written Qur'an is called the mushaf. Another surah says none touch it but the purified, and jurists drew a rule from it: handle the mushaf in a state of ritual purity, with wudu, though some read the verse differently. It's kept on a high shelf, above other books, never on the floor or under a pile. Some families wrap it in cloth. A worn-out copy isn't thrown away; it's buried in clean ground, or respectfully disposed of in other ways. None of that is the guarding the verse promises. God says He guards it. But people have answered that promise with their own small care.
screen: `YOU ARE MAD, THEY SAY.` · `TRULY WE, WE SENT IT; WE GUARD IT.` · `ADH-DHIKR — THE REMINDER.` · `THE MUSHAF: A HIGH SHELF, CLEAN HANDS.` · then, large: `IT IS GUARDED.`

segments.voice: If there's a copy of the Qur'an nearby, look at where it sits: high and clean, or under a pile of mail? If you'd like, give it an honored place; if you don't have one, think of a book or object that holds something precious for your family. If you pray, recite one short surah you know by heart.
Adh-dhikr. The Reminder, one of the Qur'an's names for itself: 15:9 says God sent it down and God will guard it. Today's word.
Your line: it is guarded. Not on your shoulders. Day four hundred forty-eight, and a week complete.

original.note: Arabic: "surely guardians," the last word of 15:9, from h-f-z, the root of hafiz.

trapdoor: what you thought: God promises the book won't be lost.
what it means: a promise to a mocked Prophet that the message doesn't depend on him, answered by believers with their own care.
what a scholar hears: 15:9 stacks emphasis (inna, nahnu, inna, la-); it answers the taunt of 15:6–7; the purity rule for the mushaf rests mainly on 56:79 and is debated by a minority.

chat.says: What does it mean that God will guard the Qur'an?
options: 15:9 says God sent the Reminder and God guards it; people's care answers that.
It means only memorizers may hold a copy, so no one else can harm it.
It means the Qur'an needs no care at all, so how it's kept doesn't matter.
chat.meaning: Verse nine: it is We who sent down the Reminder, and We who guard it. People answer that promise with small care, like a high shelf.
